title: POISONOUS SNAKES WERE KILLING ISRAEL—THEN GOD COMMANDED MOSES TO MAKE A BRONZE SNAKE. WHY WOULD GOD USE THE IMAGE OF WHAT WAS KILLING THEM TO SAVE THEIR LIVES?
paragraphs: POISONOUS SNAKES WERE KILLING ISRAEL—THEN GOD COMMANDED MOSES TO MAKE A BRONZE SNAKE. WHY WOULD GOD USE THE IMAGE OF WHAT WAS KILLING THEM TO SAVE THEIR LIVES?

They were dying from venom in their bodies. But something even more dangerous had already poisoned their hearts. Thousands of years later, Jesus revealed why this terrifying moment in the wilderness was pointing to Him—and what it means for every sinner who has ever wondered whether they have gone too far to be forgiven.
What if the very thing you are ashamed to admit is killing you spiritually is the very thing Jesus is calling you to bring into the light?
Imagine lying on the burning sand, struggling to breathe.

Your body is trembling. Your skin is burning. Somewhere nearby, a mother is crying over her child. A father is desperately trying to help his family. People are screaming. Others are praying. The camp that once echoed with complaints is now filled with the sound of human suffering.
And then someone shouts something almost impossible to believe.
“Look at the snake!”
Not run from it.
Not fight it.
Not crush it.
Look at it.
A bronze serpent has been raised above the camp, and the very people who were dying from snakebites are being told that if they look at it, they will live.
It sounds strange.
Almost offensive to human reasoning.
But what makes this story even more astonishing is that Jesus Christ Himself would later bring it up while explaining one of the greatest truths in the entire Bible.
The truth about why He came.
The truth about salvation.
The truth about the cross.
And perhaps the truth about the condition of your own heart right now.
Because sometimes the most dangerous poison is not the one that enters your body.
It is the one you have allowed to settle into your soul.
The story begins in Numbers 21:4–9.

Israel had already witnessed miracles that generations would talk about. God had delivered them from Egyptian slavery. The Red Sea had opened before them. Bread had come from heaven. Water had flowed in the wilderness.
They had seen enough evidence of God's faithfulness to fill a lifetime.
Yet they were tired.
Their journey was difficult. Their destination seemed far away. The route around Edom had discouraged them, and their patience was disappearing.
Numbers 21:4 says, in the King James Version:
“And the soul of the people was much discouraged because of the way.”
That sentence deserves more attention than we usually give it.
They were not merely physically exhausted.
Their souls were discouraged.

The Hebrew describes their inner impatience using the expression וַתִּקְצַר נֶפֶשׁ־הָעָם (vattiqtsar nefesh-ha'am), conveying that the people's spirit had grown short or impatient because of the journey.
They had reached the place where waiting felt unbearable.
And isn't that where many of our worst spiritual decisions begin?
Not when everything is falling apart all at once.
But when we have been waiting too long.
Praying too long.
Struggling too long.
Trying to understand why God has not answered the way we expected.
You believed God would restore your marriage by now.
You thought the addiction would have lost its grip.
You expected the financial pressure to ease.
You prayed for your child to come home.
You begged God to heal something nobody else even knows is broken.
And somewhere between the first prayer and the hundredth unanswered question, your heart began to change.
You still believed God existed.
But you began questioning whether He cared.
You still attended church.
But your worship became mechanical.
You still knew the language of faith.
But privately, bitterness was growing.
That is why this ancient wilderness story feels painfully modern.
Because Israel's problem was not simply that the journey was hard.
It was that hardship began reshaping how they spoke about the God who had rescued them.
Numbers 21:5 records their accusation:

“And the people spake against God, and against Moses, Wherefore have ye brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? for there is no bread, neither is there any water; and our soul loatheth this light bread.”
Read those final words again.
“Our soul loatheth this light bread.”
They were speaking contemptuously about the provision God had given them.
The manna that had sustained them became something they despised.
The miracle they once needed became the blessing they now resented.
And here is a question that might hurt more than we expect.
Have you ever become so consumed with what God has not given you that you stopped thanking Him for what He already has?
The marriage you once prayed for has become the marriage you constantly criticize.
The job you once celebrated has become the job you resent.
The ordinary days you once begged God to let you live have become days you barely appreciate.
This does not mean suffering is imaginary or that believers must pretend everything is fine.
Scripture gives us many faithful examples of lament. Job cried out in anguish. David poured out his confusion in the Psalms. Even Jesus prayed in Gethsemane with profound sorrow.
There is a difference between bringing your pain honestly before God and allowing pain to become contempt toward God.
Israel crossed that line.
And what happened next was terrifying.
Numbers 21:6 says:
“And the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people; and much people of Israel died.”
Stop there.
This is not a comfortable verse.
It does not fit easily into the kind of Christianity that speaks endlessly about blessings while refusing to acknowledge God's holiness.
The Lord sent serpents among the people.
The Hebrew expression הַנְּחָשִׁים הַשְּׂרָפִים (hannechashim haseraphim) is commonly rendered “fiery serpents.”
The description may refer to the burning effects of their bites, although the passage does not explain the exact species or the full reason for the term.
What Scripture makes unmistakably clear is that the bites were deadly.
People died.
Families suffered.
The rebellion that had seemed like ordinary complaining was suddenly exposed as something far more serious.
And we need to be careful here.

This passage describes a particular divine judgment in Israel's history. It does not give us permission to look at every sick person, grieving family, or suffering believer and declare that God is punishing them for a specific sin.
Jesus Himself rejected that simplistic assumption in John 9:1–3.
Not every tragedy is a punishment for personal wrongdoing.
But Numbers 21 does teach something we desperately need to remember.
God's grace does not make sin harmless, and God's love does not make His holiness negotiable.
We live in a world that often treats sin as a minor inconvenience.
Pride becomes self-confidence.
Greed becomes ambition.
Lust becomes personal freedom.
Unforgiveness becomes protecting our peace.
Gossip becomes sharing concerns.
And bitterness becomes something we believe we have earned the right to carry.
But changing the name of a poison does not change what it does.
A serpent does not become harmless because you refuse to call it dangerous.
And sin does not become holy because society has learned to celebrate it.
Some people are being slowly destroyed by habits they continue to defend.
Others are carrying secret guilt beneath a polished public image.
There are people reading this who have mastered the art of appearing spiritually healthy while privately falling apart.
You know how to smile in church.
You know when to say amen.
You know which Bible verses to post.
But when the room is quiet and nobody is watching, you know there are things in your life that need to be surrendered.
And perhaps the most frightening part is how easily we learn to live with what is hurting us.
Until one day, we can no longer pretend.
For Israel, that moment came when the serpents began biting.
Suddenly, the people who had accused God recognized their sin.
Numbers 21:7 says:

“Therefore the people came to Moses, and said, We have sinned, for we have spoken against the LORD, and against thee; pray unto the LORD, that he take away the serpents from us. And Moses prayed for the people.”
Four words.
“We have sinned.”
No elaborate excuse.
No blaming the weather.
No arguing that the journey had been unfair.
They confessed what they had done.
There is something beautiful about that moment, even in the middle of such terrible suffering.
The people who had spoken against Moses now came asking him to intercede for them.
And Moses prayed.
He did not celebrate their pain.
He did not tell them they deserved to suffer.
He did not use their desperation to humiliate them.
He interceded.
What a remarkable picture of mercy.
But it also points us toward someone greater than Moses.
Jesus Christ, our great High Priest, who intercedes for His people (Hebrews 7:25).
Maybe you need to hear this today.
You do not have to manufacture a perfect confession before coming to God.
You do not have to make your life presentable before admitting it is broken.
You can stop hiding.
You can tell the truth.
You can confess the bitterness, the pride, the secret compromise, the unbelief, the resentment, the things you have done and the things you have allowed to take root in your heart.
First John 1:9 tells us that God is faithful and just to forgive those who confess their sins and cleanse them from unrighteousness.
That promise is not permission to continue sinning without repentance.
It is an invitation to stop running from the only One who can forgive and restore you.
But what happened next in the wilderness is the part of the story that has puzzled readers for centuries.
God did not simply tell Moses to destroy every serpent.
He gave him an unexpected command.
Numbers 21:8 says:
“And the LORD said unto Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live.”
A serpent.
Made by human hands.
Lifted above the camp.
And the dying were told to look.
Why?
Why would the Lord use the image of the very creature that had brought such suffering?
Why not a lamb?
Why not an angel?
Why not a symbol that looked more obviously comforting?
The passage does not explicitly explain why God chose that particular image.
But it tells us exactly what God commanded and what happened when the people obeyed.
Numbers 21:9 says:
“And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived.”

The King James Version calls the material “brass,” while many modern translations use “bronze.” The Hebrew word נְחֹשֶׁת (nechoshet) can refer to copper or a copper alloy, commonly rendered bronze in this passage.
And the word used for looking in verse 9 is related to the Hebrew verb נָבַט (navat), meaning to look or regard.
The passage does not say the people healed themselves.
It does not say the metal possessed magical power.
It does not say they had to earn their healing by proving they were better than everyone else.
God appointed the means by which they would live.
They were bitten.
They were dying.
And God told them to look.
Imagine one of those wounded Israelites lying on the ground.
His body is weakening.
His family is frightened.
Someone tells him that Moses has lifted a bronze serpent and that God has promised life to those who look.
He might have argued.
He might have demanded an explanation.
He might have insisted that something so simple could never help someone in such desperate condition.
But the text tells us that those who looked at the serpent lived.
Not because bronze could remove venom.
Not because human sight had supernatural power.
But because the Lord had spoken, and His promise was trustworthy.
And now comes the moment that changes how we understand the entire story.
More than a thousand years later, Jesus spoke with a religious leader named Nicodemus.
Nicodemus knew the Scriptures.
He understood Israel's history.
He knew the law.
But Jesus told him that he needed to be born again.
And then Jesus brought him back to the wilderness.
Back to the serpents.
Back to the bronze image lifted above dying people.
John 3:14–15 records Jesus saying:
“And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.”
There it is.
The connection that makes this account far more than a strange Old Testament miracle.
Jesus Himself connected the lifted bronze serpent with His own being lifted up.
The Greek phrase ὑψωθῆναι δεῖ (hypsōthēnai dei) in John 3:14 conveys that the Son of Man must be lifted up.
This was not an accidental event in the life of Jesus.
His crucifixion was not an unforeseen disaster that forced God to improvise a rescue plan.
Christ came to accomplish the saving purpose of God.
John's Gospel repeatedly uses the language of Jesus being lifted up in connection with His death and its significance (John 8:28; 12:32–33).
The Israelites were dying from serpent bites.
Humanity is under the deadly power of sin.
God provided a means of rescue in the wilderness.
And God has provided the ultimate Savior in His Son.
But we must understand the comparison carefully.
Jesus was not a serpent. He was not sinful. He did not become morally evil on the cross.
Scripture declares that He was without sin (Hebrews 4:15).
The bronze serpent was an appointed sign in a particular historical act of deliverance. Christ is the sinless Savior to whom that event pointed.
Second Corinthians 5:21 says:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
Jesus bore the burden of our sin without ever becoming a sinner.
First Peter 2:24 tells us that He bore our sins in His own body on the tree.
Isaiah 53 speaks of the suffering Servant bearing the iniquities of others.
At Calvary, the innocent One willingly suffered for the guilty.
The holy One gave Himself for sinners.
The One who deserved no condemnation endured the cross so that those who trust Him could receive forgiveness and life.
And here is what should leave every human heart trembling.
The people in the wilderness looked toward the sign God provided because they wanted to live. We are called to look to Jesus in faith because He alone gives eternal life.
Not merely a few more years on earth.
Not simply temporary relief from suffering.
Eternal life.
Reconciliation with God.
Forgiveness of sins.
A new heart.
A new beginning.
A future that death itself cannot ultimately destroy.
Do you see why Jesus brought up this story?
Because the wilderness was revealing something humanity would never be able to solve on its own.
We are not merely wounded people who need better habits.
We are sinners who need a Savior.
We cannot cleanse our guilt through good intentions.
We cannot undo our rebellion by comparing ourselves to someone worse.
We cannot earn our way into God's favor by stacking religious activities high enough to hide our failures.
We need grace.
And grace has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Now think about the person in Israel who was bitten.
What if he had said, “I will look when I feel stronger”?
What if he had said, “I will look after I prove I deserve to live”?
What if he had said, “I will look when I understand every detail of how this works”?
The command was not to become healthy first.
The command was to look toward what God had provided.
And this is where the Gospel becomes deeply personal.
Some of you have been postponing surrender to Christ because you believe you must first become worthy of Him.
You keep telling yourself that you will return to God when you have conquered that secret sin.
When you have repaired your reputation.
When you have learned to pray properly.
When you have stopped falling into the same old patterns.
When you have finally become the kind of person you think Jesus would accept.
But that is not how salvation works.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that we are saved by grace through faith, not by works.
And Romans 5:8 tells us that Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
That does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
Jesus calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel (Mark 1:15).
It means repentance is not a performance designed to purchase His love.
It is the honest turning of a sinner toward the Savior who alone can rescue them.
You do not come to Christ because you have already made yourself clean.
You come because you cannot cleanse yourself.
You do not come because your past is impressive.
You come because His mercy is greater than your guilt.
And perhaps that is the sentence someone reading this has been waiting years to believe.
Your past is real.
Your sin matters.
The consequences of your choices may still need to be faced.
But your story does not have to end where your rebellion began.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing justice or excusing harm.
But by doing what only He can do.
Forgiving repentant sinners.
Restoring the broken.
Making the spiritually dead alive.
Transforming people who could never transform themselves.
And the Gospel does not stop at the cross.
Jesus rose from the dead.
The Savior who was lifted up in suffering is now the risen Lord.
His resurrection is the declaration that death has not won and that His saving work was not defeated.
First Corinthians 15:3–4 places His death for our sins, burial, and resurrection at the heart of the Gospel.
That is the hope we preach.
Not a religious technique.
Not a motivational philosophy.
Not a promise that believers will never suffer again.
A crucified and risen Savior.
And the astonishing thing is that immediately after Jesus speaks about Moses lifting up the serpent, John's Gospel gives us one of the most beloved declarations in all Scripture.
John 3:16:
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.”
Notice that word.
Whosoever.
The Greek is πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων (pas ho pisteuōn), meaning everyone who believes.
The promise is not restricted to people with spotless reputations.
Not limited to those raised in Christian homes.
Not reserved for those who have never wandered.
The invitation to believe in Christ goes out to sinners who desperately need Him.
The person trapped in secret shame.
The father who knows he has failed his family.
The mother who cries after everyone else is asleep.
The young person who feels spiritually numb.
The church member who has learned how to look faithful without living honestly.
The believer who has fallen and wonders whether restoration is possible.
The person who has never opened a Bible but somehow found these words today.
You are not being invited to admire a religious symbol from a distance.
You are being called to trust the living Christ.
And faith in Christ is more than merely acknowledging that He existed.
The Greek verb πιστεύω (pisteuō) means to believe or trust. In John's Gospel, believing in Jesus involves relying on Him as the One God has sent.
It is not a magic phrase.
It is not a transaction purchased by emotion.
It is trusting the Savior who died and rose again.
And if that trust is real, it does not leave our relationship with sin unchanged.
The grace that forgives also teaches us to turn away from ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12).
The Savior who receives us also calls us to follow Him.
Which brings us to another sobering part of the bronze serpent's history.
The story did not end in Numbers 21.
Centuries later, the same bronze serpent became an object of improper worship.
Second Kings 18:4 tells us that King Hezekiah destroyed it because the people of Israel had been burning incense to it.
They had taken something God once used as an instrument of deliverance and turned it into an object of religious devotion.
Think about that.
A reminder of God's mercy had become an idol.
A sign had been treated as though it deserved the worship that belongs to God alone.
And that warning is just as relevant today.
We can become more attached to Christian symbols than to Christ.
More protective of our religious traditions than obedient to Scripture.
More concerned with the popularity of a ministry than with the truth of the Gospel.
More impressed by a preacher's personality than by the Savior being preached.
Even something originally associated with God's work can become spiritually dangerous when it takes the place that belongs to Him.
The bronze serpent was never meant to replace the God who healed. And no Christian ministry should ever replace the Christ it proclaims.
That includes Gospel Warrior.
Our purpose is to keep directing hearts to Jesus.
To His Word.
To His cross.
To His resurrection.
To the transforming power of His grace.
Because a ministry has lost its way when people remember the messenger but forget the Savior.
And that is why I want to speak to you personally for a moment.
If you have read this far, there may be a reason this story has stayed with you.
Perhaps you recognize something of Israel's impatience in your own life.
Perhaps you have been angry with God.
Perhaps you have allowed disappointment to turn into bitterness.
Perhaps you have spent months trying to hide a struggle that has quietly been consuming your peace.
Or perhaps you are simply exhausted from pretending that everything is okay.
You do not need to announce every private detail to the world.
But you do need to be honest before God.
And where appropriate, you may need the help of a trusted pastor, mature believer, or someone who can walk with you toward healing and accountability.
Please hear this.
The Lord does not ask you to make your wounds impressive.
He calls you to come to Him in truth.
You can begin with a prayer as simple as this:

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned against You. I have complained when I should have trusted. I have hidden things I should have confessed. I have tried to control what I should have surrendered. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Teach me to turn from my sin and follow You. I cannot save myself. My hope is in You alone. Amen.”
There is no special power in repeating those exact words.
The power belongs to the Savior to whom we pray.
And if you have already trusted Christ but have wandered, remember that the call to repentance is not only for the day you first believed.
The Christian life is a life of continuing faith, confession, obedience, and dependence on grace.
You may still have battles to fight.
You may need to repair relationships.
You may need to seek forgiveness from someone you have hurt.
You may need to break patterns that have controlled you for years.
And some consequences will not disappear overnight.
But you do not have to fight those battles while pretending you can save yourself.
Look to Christ.
Return to His Word.
Pray.
Walk in fellowship with believers who will tell you the truth and help you grow.
And when you stumble, do not make peace with the sin.
Return to the Savior.
There is one more detail about the wilderness story that I cannot get out of my mind.
Imagine how differently the people might have responded to the raised serpent.
Some may have been near it.
Others far away.
Some may have been strong enough to stand.
Others may have barely been able to lift their heads.
The passage does not give us those individual stories.
But it does tell us that the promise extended to those who had been bitten and looked at what God had provided.
And that makes me think about how differently people arrive at the foot of the cross.
Some come with years of religious knowledge.
Others come knowing almost nothing about the Bible.
Some come after a lifetime of obvious rebellion.
Others come after years of respectable, hidden pride.
Some arrive with tears.
Others are so emotionally exhausted they can barely feel anything.
But none of us comes with a righteousness sufficient to save ourselves.
We come needing Christ.
And He is sufficient.
That is why the invitation of the Gospel must never be reduced to a demand for money, an emotional performance, or an attempt to impress other Christians.
Yet when grace genuinely takes hold of a person's heart, it often changes how that person thinks about generosity, service, and the spread of God's Word.
We begin to ask a different question.
Not, “How little can I give and still feel religious?”
But, “Lord, how can I faithfully use what You have entrusted to me?”
For some, that means sharing the Gospel with a neighbor.

For others, it means encouraging a struggling believer, discipling a younger Christian, serving in a local church, helping someone in need, or supporting trustworthy ministries that teach Scripture faithfully.

And if Gospel Warrior has helped you understand God's Word, strengthened you during a difficult season, or encouraged you to return to Christ, you can help us continue making these resources available.
Not because every share guarantees someone will be saved.
Salvation belongs to the Lord.
But because sharing biblical truth creates another opportunity for someone to hear about Jesus.
You may never know who is silently reading your posts.
Someone in your family may be struggling with guilt.
An old friend may have stopped attending church.
A coworker may be wondering whether God still cares.
Someone who has never told you about their pain may read a single paragraph that encourages them to open the Bible and seek Christ.
And if one particular person comes to mind as you read this, consider tagging them with kindness or sending the article privately.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to expose their struggles.
But to remind them that they are not beyond the reach of God's mercy.
What part of this story confronted your heart the most—the complaining, the consequences of sin, the confession, or the invitation to look to Christ?
You can share your testimony, a Scripture that has strengthened you, or simply write “Christ is still healing me” if you are learning to walk in repentance and grace.
You do not need to reveal anything too private to be welcomed into a conversation about God's faithfulness.
And if someone else shares a struggle, respond with compassion. Pray for them. Point them toward Scripture. Let the comments become a place where truth and grace are both taken seriously.
We want to keep opening Scripture together.
Not merely collecting inspiring quotes.
Not merely chasing emotional moments.
But learning what God's Word actually says, understanding it in context, and allowing the truth of Christ to reshape how we live.
These free resources are part of our desire to make biblical encouragement and discipleship accessible to more people.
And for those who are able and willing to help sustain and expand this work, there is another opportunity.
Your monthly contribution can be part of your intentional Christian giving—an offering toward Gospel-centered ministry work.
But it is important to keep our giving biblical.
Scripture calls believers to generosity that is willing, thoughtful, and sincere.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That means giving should never be driven by guilt or spiritual intimidation.
It is an additional opportunity to participate in ministry support as God provides and as you freely choose.
Every ministry needs people who pray.
People who share.
People who encourage.
People who serve.
And, when possible, people who give.
These products are not what make anyone more spiritual.
They are simply additional resources and expressions of encouragement for those who find them useful.
The greater purpose remains the same.
To keep the Gospel visible.
To make Scripture accessible.
To encourage repentance, faith, discipleship, and spiritual growth.
To help people move from knowing about Jesus to faithfully following Him.
Pray that Scripture will never be twisted merely to attract attention.
Pray that truth will never be compromised for popularity.
Pray that people will not simply become followers of a page but genuine disciples of Jesus.
Because the ultimate goal is not to build an audience around Gospel Warrior.
It is to point people to the Savior who is worthy of every heart.
Now, before you leave, I want you to return with me one final time to that wilderness.
Imagine the camp.
The fear.
The cries.
The dying.
The serpent raised on a pole.
And the astonishing mercy of God, who provided a way for bitten people to live.
Then look beyond the wilderness.
Look toward Calvary.
See the Son of God, innocent and holy, willingly enduring the cross.
Hear the words of Jesus in John 19:30:
“It is finished.”
The Greek word is τετέλεσται (tetelestai).
It conveys completion or accomplishment.
Jesus was declaring that His work had reached its appointed fulfillment.
And although the story of the bronze serpent and the crucifixion are not identical in every detail, Jesus Himself gave us the connection we must not miss.
The Son of Man was lifted up so that those who believe in Him may have eternal life.
The wilderness healing was temporary.
The salvation Christ gives is eternal.
The bronze serpent could never forgive sins.
Jesus can.
The bronze serpent could never conquer death.
Jesus rose victorious over the grave.
The bronze serpent was eventually destroyed because people had turned it into an idol.
But Jesus Christ is the risen Lord, worthy of worship forever.
And now the question is no longer simply why God told Moses to make a bronze serpent.
The deeper question is this.
If God has revealed His Son as the only Savior, why would we keep looking everywhere else for the life that only He can give?
Why keep hiding behind pride?
Why keep defending what Scripture calls sin?
Why keep treating the cross as an interesting religious story instead of facing what it means for your own life?
Why keep postponing repentance as though tomorrow has been promised?
The same Jesus who spoke to Nicodemus still calls people to believe.
The same Lord who forgave sinners still calls us to turn from sin.
The same Savior who died at Calvary is alive.
And His invitation is not limited to people whose stories look beautiful.
It reaches into shame.
Into failure.
Into rebellion.
Into regret.
Into the parts of our lives we would rather nobody ever discover.
Not to tell us that sin never mattered.
But to show us just how much His mercy cost.
So if this message has stirred something in you, do not let the emotion be the end of it.
Open your Bible.
Read Numbers 21:4–9.
Read John 3:1–21.
Read Romans 5.
Ask God to expose what needs to change.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Trust the Christ who died and rose again.
And take the next faithful step.
Maybe that means returning to prayer tonight.
Maybe it means finally telling someone the truth.
Maybe it means asking forgiveness.
Maybe it means finding a faithful local church where you can grow in Scripture and Christian fellowship.
Maybe it means sharing this article with someone you love because you want them to hear the Gospel too.
And maybe, for the first time in a very long time, it means letting go of the exhausting attempt to save yourself.
Because you were never meant to be your own savior.
Christ has already accomplished what you never could.
I pray that when you remember this story, you will not remember only the snakes.
You will remember the mercy.
You will remember the cross.
You will remember the Savior.
And you will remember that no sinner is rescued by pretending the poison is harmless.
We are rescued by the grace of God through faith in Jesus Christ.
The poison revealed how desperately they needed to live. The cross reveals how deeply we need the One who died so that sinners could live forever.
